Pele Yoetz 274:2: Therefore how good is companionship for Torah study, for iron sharpens iron, and even in mundane matters, one who listens to counsel is wise, and salvation lies in an abundance of counselors (Proverbs 11:14), and two are better than one (Ecclesiastes 4:9). And if he wishes to rely on his own knowledge because he has no one to speak with, let him do this: perhaps there is hope — that for every matter that arises in his mind at first glance, whether in Torah or in mundane matters, he should seek and search to refute himself between himself and himself, as though a man were standing to confront him, seeking with all his strength to knock down his reasoning; through the argument the truth will be clarified in this way, and perhaps he will arrive at the way of truth. But if he seeks only to uphold his own opinion, who can understand his errors, for there is nothing as easy as a person being mistaken in his own imagination, and especially for us, orphans of orphans, great study is needed, and mercy should be sought from the One who grants man knowledge, that He guide him in the way of truth.
Pele Yoetz 275:1: Aniyah (Congregational Response) — The congregational responses — “Amen,” “yehei shmei rabba,” “Barechu,” and “Kedushah” — are matters that stand at the summit of the world, yet people treat them disrespectfully; some are like the deaf who do not hear and like mutes who do not open their mouths to answer, and some answer with a truncated, hurried, or orphaned “Amen.” And the severity involved is known, for they were strict in the holy Zohar, Parashat Vayelech (p. 286 approx.), regarding one who does not answer “Amen” — wonder of wonders — to the point that they said that whoever disgraces the response of “Amen,” and over many “Amens” that have been lost, he is judged in Gehinnom and brought down to that lowest chamber and lost, never to rise forever, Heaven have mercy. And they further said there in the holy Zohar that whoever hears a blessing and does not have proper intention regarding it, of him it is said (I Samuel 2:30), “And those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed.” And the commentators explained that this means it is not enough merely to answer “Amen” — one must intend it according to what it is: if it is over praise, he should intend in saying “Amen” that he means “true,” and if it is over a petition, he should intend in saying “Amen” that he means “so may it be [His] will,” and if that blessing has both praise and petition, he should intend in saying “Amen” both “true” and “so may it be [His] will.” And let him intend that “Amen” numerically equals the Tetragrammaton plus Adonai, and intend the interweaving — except that in blessings he should place the letters of the Tetragrammaton first, and in the Kaddish he should place the letters of Adonai first. And one who does not have this intention, of him it is said, “And those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed.” Let all who mourn mourn over this, for who is clean of this? In any case, let a man be firm in strengthening himself to perform the commandment properly, to give one more delight to his Creator. And let him be careful about a hurried, truncated, or orphaned “Amen,” whose punishment is explained in the Talmud (Berachot 47a) and the halachic authorities (Orach Chaim, sec. 124, para. 8) — examine them and guard your soul greatly if you are a person of true feeling.
Pele Yoetz 275:2: Likewise, in responding to Kedushah one must have great intention, for it is an awesome praise that the angels on high answer in dread and say in fear. Let him close his eyes and lift them upward, and let him make three little leaps when saying “Kadosh, Kadosh, Kadosh,” and intend to fulfill the commandment “And I shall be sanctified among the children of Israel” (Leviticus 22:32), and intend that he is ready and prepared to fulfill this commandment by giving his life for the sanctification of the Name, whenever the opportunity comes to him. And let him intend the meaning explained in the Aramaic translation: “Holy above, holy below, holy forever.”
Pele Yoetz 275:3: And let him intend, in every response, that there are deep and supernal mysteries, and he is building his chambers in heaven and giving great delight to his Creator. Go and learn from the reward involved, for they said (Shabbat 119b) that whoever answers “Amen, yehei shmei rabba” with all his strength — and the commentators explained this to mean with all his intention and the movement of his inner limbs — they tear up his decree and forgive all his sins. And there are many such good virtues explained in the Talmud and the Midrashim, and especially in the holy book of the Zohar (Parashat Pinchas, p. 220 approx.). Therefore it is fitting for every God-fearing person to be firm in strengthening himself with great vigor to respond and intend properly, according to his knowledge, one more time. And if those who fail to respond knew the greatness of the reward for the congregational responses of “Amen,” “yehei shmei rabba,” “Barechu,” and “Kedushah,” they would pursue going to hear and respond, as one pursues a partridge in the mountains, and would rejoice over one response like one who finds abundant spoil. But the difficulty is that they do not know what this commandment is, and its severity, and the greatness of its reward. May the good Name grant them atonement, and plant in our hearts His love and fear, to do His will as He wills, Amen, so may it be [His] will.
Pele Yoetz 276:1: Atzlut (Laziness) — Laziness is an exceedingly bad trait for body and soul, as is known, and famous matters need no proof. This is a gift of God and is a natural disposition in a person: there is one whose nature is to be a vigorous man of many deeds, diligent and rewarded, and there is one whose nature is to be sluggish and lazy. Now, regarding mundane matters, this trait is bad for a man, and all the more so for a woman, who must watch over the ways of her household (Proverbs 31:27) — if she is lazy, woe to her and woe to her household, and quarrels come upon her, a daughter-in-law with her mother-in-law, and one woman envies and hates and rivals another; but in any case, there is not so much sin involved in this. And if the Lord has graced him with wealth, laziness is not so noticeable and makes no impression, since his work is done through others; but regarding matters of Heaven, if he has this laziness, it is a chronic evil. And even though this is his nature from the womb and from conception, this is not a way to remove him from transgression, for it is within a person's power to reverse his nature and change it through toil and labor, and by accustoming himself to the opposite extreme he can arrive at the middle path, and a person rules over his own spirit, and whatever he desires he can do, and the reward is according to the pain (Avot, end of ch. 5), and let him build a fence for himself through penalties. And let a man be firm in strengthening himself through strategies, to be light as an eagle and swift as a deer to do the will of our Father in Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 277:1: Atzvut (Sadness/Melancholy) — Sadness is also a bad trait, destroying both soul and body, for it comes from the root of the serpent, for the serpent's food is dust, and sadness comes from the element of dust. It is the trait of the “other woman” [a euphemism for the Sitra Achra in Kabbalah], and this man should divorce her [i.e., reject the trait], for her name is truly “wailing,” and she brings one to seminal emission, and a mnemonic is fixed: “the sad one emits seed.” And many evils follow from it, for one who serves the Lord with sadness and a scowling face [transgresses], and Scripture says (Deuteronomy 28:47), “Because you did not serve the Lord your God with joy and gladness of heart, out of the abundance of all things.” And it causes strife and quarrel, for even if peace is spoken to them, at that very moment they are ready for war.
Pele Yoetz 277:2: Now, this trait of sadness sometimes comes to a person from an impure mishap that befell him in his body or his possessions, and sometimes from having clothed himself in pride, so that as soon as anything at all is done against his will, or something seems to him according to his own opinion not befitting his honor, immediately fire burns within him and his wrath blazes in him; and when he cannot say anything or take revenge, his sadness is his own doing, in such a way that sadness is the offspring of pride and anger — what comes from the impure is impure.
Pele Yoetz 277:3: And the man who is pure should be firm with valor and strength in pushing this trait away from himself with pure thoughts: if the sadness comes to him because something was done against his will, and his will was not fulfilled as he wished, let him humble himself and reason, “What am I and what is my life, and what does it give or add if a man like myself, who is like a mere breath, honors me or disgraces me — all is vanity.” And if the sadness comes to him due to some mishap, let him reason that it is not mere chance, but the decree of the Creator for his own benefit, for “whom the Lord loves He rebukes” (Proverbs 3:12), and let his heart rejoice and his glory exult that the Lord loves him. And why should a living man complain — let him overcome his sins (Lamentations 3:39), which caused anger and pain to the exalted and uplifted King. And this too is not at all times, but rather at a time when he recalls his own debts [sins] and at a time when he recalls the destruction of the Temple, destroyed through our many sins — then all sadness is permitted, and whoever increases sadness in his heart with grief and sighing, weeping and moaning, is to be praised; but at other times, and especially at a time of serving the Lord, let him forget his sadness and his anger and be altogether joyful and glad of heart.
Pele Yoetz 277:4: And the author of Sefer HaBrit already wrote that whoever has understanding will find no room to be sad about anything whatsoever, for sadness can only apply to one of two things: either something that has a remedy or something that has no remedy. If there is a remedy, why should he be sad? Let him make the remedy and be saved. And if there is no remedy, what benefit is there in being sad? Behold, King David, peace be upon him, when his son died, said, “Set bread on the table,” for he said, “What benefit is there for a man to afflict his soul — can I bring him back? I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me” (II Samuel 12:23). And further, let a man reflect, at a time of sadness, over the events of the age, that there is no good in the world like the good of our having a Torah of truth, good statutes and commandments. And let him picture himself as one who has a thousand thousand gold dinars and loses a small perutah about which he does not worry. And if he is sad over mundane matters, or becomes angry according to its severity, this is comparable to one who loses a perutah and throws away abundant gold and fine gold over it — so it is with this matter. This and more should the living take to heart, to remove evil from his flesh, and be joyful and glad of heart, and his flesh shall dwell securely.
Pele Yoetz 277:5: And there is a kind of sadness that comes from the illness of an overpowering black bile, called in our language melancholia or “milanconia.” This trait is found much among some of the wealthy, especially on the night after the holy Shabbat, and in the morning when they rise from their sleep, until they drink coffee and raise smoke. They need to seek a remedy for their affliction, for their evil is great and the evil of those who sit in their company and serve them. Let him turn his mind to things that gladden the heart, and how good it is to engage in Torah, for “the precepts of the Lord are upright, gladdening the heart” (Psalms 19:9). And even if his heart does not turn to it and he cannot take a book in his hand, let him press himself, for even if its beginning is painful, in the end his heart will rejoice, provided he is wise and understands what he is studying and engages in dialectics with wisdom, or studies aggadic matters, or matters that come from midrash, and thereby Israel shall rejoice in its Maker.
Pele Yoetz 278:1: Azut (Boldness) — The saying of the Tanna Yehuda ben Teima is known (Avot 5:20): “Be bold as a leopard,” etc., “to do the will of your Father in Heaven.” And they said (ibid. 2:5), “The shy one does not learn.” And a person refrains from doing several commandments and upright practices because of shame, and especially the commandment of rebuke, which has almost been forgotten from Israel, and there is no one in this generation who rebukes; for if one sees a wealthy and esteemed man eating and drinking without a blessing, or speaking in the synagogue during prayer, or transgressing other transgressions and prohibitions that many have trampled upon and made as though permitted, doing them publicly, he is ashamed and afraid to approach and rebuke, and shuts his eyes from seeing, and does not open his mouth to chirp — and many such evils a person transgresses against his own understanding and against his Maker's will because of shame. And our teacher Rabbi Moshe Alshech has already explained that this is the meaning of the verse (Jeremiah 3:24), “And shame has devoured the labor of our fathers.” And the man who is a Jew must weigh the loss of a commandment against its reward, and reason that it is better to be embarrassed in this world than to be shamed in the World to Come before thousands upon thousands and myriads of holy camps, not to mention the punishment he will bring upon his own soul — better that he be called a fool all his days than be wicked before the Omnipresent for even one hour.
Pele Yoetz 278:2: And all the more so those who transgress commandments because of shame before gentiles, such as not wearing a tallit and tefillin on the road, and not praying properly, and those who wear leather shoes on Tisha B'Av and Yom Kippur and the like — this is vanity and vexation of spirit, for in any case we are “a taunt to our neighbors, a scorn and derision to those around us” (Psalms 79:4), so why should we worry about the mockery of the complacent, “the scorn of the arrogant” (ibid. 123:4)? For all the nations walk each in the name of its god, and we walk in the name of the Lord our God forever and ever. And King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 119:46), “And I will speak of Your testimonies before kings and not be ashamed.” And let him consider: if he could find a way to earn a thousand thousand gold dinars, he would certainly not worry about any shame regarding this world's temporal profit — how much more so for the sake of the life of the World to Come and giving delight to his Creator. And of such a matter it is said (Proverbs 2:4-5), “If you seek it as silver,” etc., “then you will understand the fear of the Lord.”
Pele Yoetz 278:3: And there is a bad kind of boldness, of which the Tanna said (Avot 5:20), “Boldness of face leads to Gehinnom.” And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Nedarim 20a), “Whoever has no shame in his face, it is known that his ancestors did not stand at Mount Sinai,” and “a mixed multitude is coming” (meaning his soul is from the people of the mixed multitude), for one of the three signs that Israel possesses is that they are bashful. And now, through our sins, the bold-faced have multiplied in this generation, and this is also the reason there is no one in this generation who rebukes, since there is no one who accepts rebuke, for a son does not honor his father, nor a servant his master; a daughter rises up against her mother, a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and the faces of elders are not honored. And if one says a word of rebuke to his fellow, he too responds with pride and scorn, harsh words like sinews, embittering words, and “little foxes that ruin the vineyards,” and because of this the modest withdraw their hand and leave the world to its own custom — woe to a generation upon which such things have fallen in its days. This is our comfort, seeing the words of our sages, of blessed memory, who said (Sotah 49b) that in the footsteps of the Messiah insolence will increase, and the face of the generation will be like the face of a dog.
Pele Yoetz 278:4: But the God-fearing man should hold to his righteous way, and command his children and his household and those who submit to his authority to have shame in their faces, and that a son honor his father and mother and everyone greater than him in wisdom and in age, and even to a man of his own standing he should not answer boldly, but rather with a gentle voice, gravity, and respect. And let him accustom his children and his students not to defy or speak wrongly with boldness of face against any person, and certainly not in the presence of great men, that they show honor before their elders (Isaiah 24:23). And even if someone strikes them or curses them, let him give his cheek to the one who strikes him and be silent. And if he wishes to state his case and clear himself of suspicion, let him speak his words with great respect.
Pele Yoetz 278:5: And especially those who sit before sages and Torah scholars themselves must be very careful to show one another this respect, and speak each word calmly and with great respect, for they said (Ecclesiastes 9:17), “The words of the wise are heard in gentleness.” And it is written (Proverbs 3:35), “The wise shall inherit honor.” And how greatly must one strengthen himself to acquire this trait, for they said (Derech Eretz Zuta 8), “Whoever has shame in his face does not sin quickly,” and is assured of being destined for the World to Come, as the Tanna said (Avot 5:20), “Shamefacedness leads to the Garden of Eden.” And know with certainty that boldness too is an offshoot of pride and anger — examine this and you will find it so. Therefore, whoever wishes to be saved from this bad trait should humble himself and subdue his anger, and strengthen himself to be like a mute, not opening his mouth, or speaking his words with a gentle voice and great respect — perhaps there is hope, and he shall turn and be healed, for one who comes to purify himself is helped [from Heaven] (Shabbat 104a).
Pele Yoetz 279:1: Amal (Toil/Labor) — This is a great principle in the Torah upon which the entire fulfillment of the Torah and all of Judaism depends, for man is born to toil (Job 5:7) in Torah and in the service of the blessed Name, for what advantage has a man in his toil that he toils under the sun (Ecclesiastes 1:3). Happy is he whose toil is in Torah, to subdue his inclination and withdraw his hand and flee from every hint of transgression, whether in thought, speech, or deed, and to fulfill every good thing, whether in thought, speech, or deed. And if a person says, “I have not labored yet I have found,” do not believe him. And it is certainly and completely true that Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses our teacher, and all the holy ones had an evil inclination just like ours, except that through great toil and labor they subdued their inclination to cling to their Maker, until in the end it turned into a friend for them and became a doer of good. And of Abraham it is said (Nehemiah 9:8), “And You found his heart faithful before You.” And King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 109:22), “And my heart is empty within me.” For only the beginnings are hard.
Pele Yoetz 279:2: And it is true that there is a difference in dispositions and natures from the womb and from conception — there is one whose conception and birth are in holiness and whose soul is a holy soul, having the help of the Almighty, and “the breath of the Almighty gives him understanding.” And there is one who was conceived in sin and whose mother brought him forth in transgression, whose soul is caught among the husks, as I wrote above under the entry Zivug. And these too are wondrous things beyond the perfect Knower, for sometimes the pure comes forth from the impure, such as Abraham our father, and the matriarchs, and Hezekiah king of Judah, and several righteous converts, pillars of the world, such as Shemayah and Avtalyon and their colleagues. And sometimes the impure comes forth from the pure, such as Esau and Ishmael and their like. But in any case, this is not a way to remove him from transgression, and it does not exempt him entirely from judgment, for even if he is treated leniently at the time of weighing according to the scale and balance of justice which is weighed according to the knowledge of the Lord, in any case, obviously, God will bring every person into judgment for whatever was in his power to do and he did not do, and for not having waged war with his evil inclination in the book of the wars of the Lord, to flee every transgression and fulfill every good thing, at least matters that depend on speech and deed — for the father does not merit the son from the womb and from conception, and it does not depend on the holiness of the soul, but rather on the matter of cleaving of thought to fear and love the Lord and cling to Him and serve Him with a whole heart, for a person has no control over his own spirit without the help of the Almighty. But this is a matter that depends on speech and deed, which is within every person's power: to subdue his inclination and nullify his own will before his Maker's will. And “though his beginning was small, his end shall greatly increase” (Job 8:7), and it will become sweet and pleasant to him, and through the sanctification of speech and deed he will merit also the sanctification of thought, for the Lord will shine His countenance upon him and send him a sanctifying helper, and the Lord will create in him a pure heart, and a spirit of knowledge and fear of the Lord will surround him and give him understanding, until he becomes one of the great ones of holiness, in such a way that every person can attain to be like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Pele Yoetz 279:3: And it is true that a person's inclination grows stronger over him every day and seeks to kill him, and were it not that the Holy One, blessed be He, helps him, he could not overcome it (Sukkah 52b; Kiddushin 30b), and one must precede trouble with prayer and seek mercy from before God regarding every matter of transgression, that He save him, and regarding every good thing, that He help him, as I have written in its place. But prayer alone does not suffice, for if a person prays all day that the Lord save him from the evil inclination and help him for the sake of the honor of His Name, yet he does not strengthen himself against his inclination, this is a vain prayer, for the Lord created the evil inclination of man's heart for his own benefit and good, so that he subdue his inclination and receive reward, for this is the whole of man; and were it not for the evil inclination, man would be like the ministering angels and would have no reward or punishment, and would have no need to come into this world, and the entire world was created only for this purpose: that they subdue their inclination and receive good reward for their toil, and according to the pain he gives delight to his Creator and receives good reward for his toil, in such a way that it is impossible to remove the heart of stone from within us until Shiloh comes, and prayer alone does not help for this matter. To what is this comparable? To a man locked in a house with his hands bound, doing no business at all, who asks for mercy all day that the Lord command the blessing to be with him — certainly his prayer bears no fruit, and the Holy One, blessed be He, does not perform a miracle through the windows of heaven to pour out blessing for him, for it is written (Deuteronomy 14:29), “So that the Lord your God may bless you in all the work of your hand that you do.” Some engagement in a craft or business is needed, and mercy should be sought that his work be blessed, and the blessing of the Lord enriches (Proverbs 10:22) — so it is with this matter. And furthermore, regarding livelihood, merit can be a factor, so that a miracle is done for him and he finds a treasure, or blessing rests in his purse and his possessions; and there are those whose work is done through others while they sit idle from work — but regarding the evil inclination, nothing entirely saves a person from his own hand; rather, he must strengthen himself and also speak supplications, and after many days he will find the help of the Almighty and will remove the spirit of impurity, for the Holy One, blessed be He, provides only assistance, for everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven (Berachot 33b), only that one who comes to purify himself is helped from Heaven (Shabbat 104a) (and I have written more on this above under the entry Chazak — see there).
Pele Yoetz 280:1: Averah (Transgression) — The saying of the Tanna is known (Avot 4:11): whoever commits one transgression acquires for himself one accuser, and it wraps around him and leads him to the Day of Judgment. And even if he transgressed only one transgression, he is included in “cursed be he who does not uphold all the words of the Torah” (Deuteronomy 27:26). And every transgression a person commits shows that he has no regard for his Maker's honor, and he will surely be punished, whether he believes that the blessed Name's glory fills the whole earth and sins before Him, or if he does not believe, in which case he is as though pushing away the feet of the Divine Presence. And since the world is judged according to its majority, one must be wary lest through a single transgression he tip the balance of the whole world toward guilt, and he will surely be punished for having caused delay of the Messiah and destruction of the world and pain to the upper and lower realms. And every transgression a person commits is as though he worships idolatry, for just as one who worships idolatry abandons the Name, the God of the world, and accepts another as his master and patron, so this one accepts his own inclination to be his judge, and it rules over him. And there are furthermore several other aspects that make the sinner liable for every single transgression, for the evil of a sinning person is great in heaven and on earth, beyond measure.
Pele Yoetz 280:2: And through our sins, there are several transgressions that many have trampled upon and made as though permitted, such as gazing at women, and all kinds of forbidden speech, slander, vulgar speech, mockery, flattery, lies, taking the Name in vain, false oaths, hurried and truncated prayers and blessings without intention, mundane talk in the synagogue, mundane talk on Shabbat, idle words, pride, anger, and many other such prohibitions and bad traits and neglect of commandments, with neglect of Torah study outweighing them all, to the point that whoever does these things feels no pain in his heart and does not regret it, and goes from evil to evil. Let the living take to heart these truly stated matters, for a transgression is grave and causes great harm to himself and to all the upper and lower worlds, and the man who is a Jew and believes in the Lord and in His holy Torah and in the words of our holy sages, of blessed memory, should tremble and take hold of himself and have regard for his Maker's honor and for all the worlds, and for his own precious soul, which is like a king's daughter, and day by day flee more and more from transgression as from a sword, and overcome his inclination, and let his heart cry out to his Father that He help him and save him from sin, more so than one who cries out and prays for his only son if he lies on a sickbed in danger of death, for the trouble of transgression is a trouble indeed — there is no trouble in the world greater than it, and of it David said (Psalms 25:17), “The troubles of my heart have enlarged; bring me out of my distresses.” And it appears to me that every trouble mentioned in the Book of Psalms refers to this matter, and for this every pious person should pray to the Lord, for He is good and upright, therefore He instructs sinners in the way [of the good].
Pele Yoetz 281:1: Ezer (Help) — Just as the Holy One, blessed be He, is found to be a very present help in troubles, so it is fitting for a person to walk in His ways and help his fellow with his body, his money, and good words, a word fitly spoken, and bear the burden together with his fellow, and not say, “Peace be upon my own soul, what is this trouble to me?” for we are all children of one man, we are brothers, and a brother is born for adversity. And the helper — God shall be his help, and his crown shall shine upon him.
Pele Yoetz 282:1: Oneg (Delight) — The virtue of one who delights in Shabbat is known, for our sages, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 118a) that they give him an inheritance without boundaries, and grant him the desires of his heart, and he is saved from subjugation to kingdoms. And they said (ibid. 119a) that the wealthy outside the Land, by what do they merit [their wealth]? Because they delight in Shabbat, as in the story of Yosef Mokir Shabbat (ibid.), and that man who ate at a table of gold, a burden for sixteen men (ibid.). And from the reward you can understand that this gives great delight to his Creator. And this is one of the matters through which extraordinary affection is made known to us: that by delighting his soul in fatness it is counted as a commandment, and he gives delight to his Creator and receives reward. Happy is one born of woman who has merited this — happy are we, how good is our portion!
Pele Yoetz 282:2: And it is true that some commentators have been precise about the saying of our sages, of blessed memory (Shabbat 118a), “Whoever delights [the object] the Shabbat” [me'aneg et haShabbat], and did not say, “Whoever delights in Shabbat” [ha'mitaneg beShabbat] — meaning the matter does not depend on his own will, on what is a delight to him; for if he delights in sitting idle or in excessive idle talk, or in increasing frivolity, this is not the delight of Shabbat, and he loses out, and even a thousand of his own pleasures should not cause him to lose the delight of Shabbat, for Sabbaths and festivals were given only for engaging in Torah. In any case, the plain meaning does not fully hold either, for everyone agrees that on Shabbat we also need “for you,” and he should hold to this and also to that — eat and drink what his soul desires to satisfy his soul, and sleep more than is chosen [i.e., preferred otherwise], for they said (Shabbat 118b), “With what does one delight it? With large fish,” etc., and the matters are ancient, and both the one who does much and the one who does little [are equal], provided he directs his heart to Heaven, for in commandments such as these, which involve delight and bodily pleasure, great strength is needed to do them for the sake of Heaven truly, not merely with lip service, wanting only to fill his belly and saying, “It is Shabbat today, eat today, drink and be merry.” And by this you shall be tested, whether you do it for the honor of Shabbat: just as on other days you do not pursue the pleasures and vanities of this world [for their own sake]. And even one who is sparing with himself on other days finds it very difficult to intend his pleasures purely for the love of the blessed Name, and this I explain: “How fair and how pleasant is love, with delights” (Song of Songs 7:7).
Pele Yoetz 282:3: And the man who is righteous and pious, upright and faithful, does not delight in anything in the world except the service of the Creator, and even one who delights [physically] should consider that this delight is to him like an affliction, only that his will is to give delight to his Creator. And certainly Shabbat was not given to be set aside for the delight of Shabbat, and not even the slightest rabbinic prohibition is permitted — not like the ignorant among the people who are lenient about several prohibitions, such as heating water or coffee through gentiles, or buying fruit from gentiles, and many other such prohibitions that have been trampled upon; it is fitting to protest against them, for this “delight” brings on affliction [a wordplay on oneg/nega]. Now, one whom the Lord has graced with wealth and possessions, who is calm and secure without any trouble or distraction, should not be praised so much for delighting in Shabbat; rather, one may truly boast when he is in pressing circumstances and many evils and troubles have found him, yet when Shabbat arrives, he presses himself to spend a little more than his means for the honor of Shabbat, being sparing on weekdays in order to add on Shabbat, and turns his mind and forgets his sadness and anger and his heart rejoices and his glory exults, and he delights his soul in fatness for the honor of the Rock of his sanctity — this man is to be praised. And according to his understanding, a man should be praised who has control over his spirit to do each thing in its proper time, not exchanging or trading it — at a time of joy, strength and joy, and at a time of sadness, sadness — and even if, God forbid, someone dear to him died before him on Shabbat and it disturbs his joy, then strength and settled, proper understanding are needed to store the trouble away in a corner until the conclusion of the holy Shabbat. And let him do likewise at every time he serves God, for one must serve Him with joy and gladness of heart — let him remove evil from his mind and picture as though his flesh dwells securely, and let him take to heart that there is no evil in the world like the evil of the destruction of the Temple, destroyed through our sins, to the point that it is said (Jeremiah 8:23), “Oh that my head were waters and my eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night.” And nevertheless, at a time of joy it is forbidden to grieve and be sad over it — rather, gladness and joy shall be attained, and sorrow and sighing shall flee (Isaiah 35:10), in a place where they are not remembered, not recalled, and do not come to mind.
Pele Yoetz 282:4: And just as it is a commandment to delight on Shabbat, on the other hand, it is good for a man not to pursue the pleasures and vanities of this world on weekdays, for it is all vanity, and after a moment, as it passes, it is as though it never was, and that pleasure is lost in a bad affair, and its end turns into an affliction, for all the judgment of the beating of the grave and the judgment of the worm like a needle are all because of pleasures. But the very person who does not indulge himself from the Sitra Achra on weekdays, only on Shabbatot and festivals, the Sitra Achra cannot rule over him, and his flesh shall dwell securely — so they said in the holy Zohar (part 2, p. 141 approx.). And in Avot DeRabbi Natan (ch. 28, near end) they said: whoever accepts the pleasures of this world is withheld from the pleasure of the World to Come. Therefore the righteous man eats to satisfy his soul with less than his need and just enough for his necessity, and food that is pleasant to his palate he withdraws his hand from, and it is accepted as an atonement for him, and he should not be particular about food but rather be satisfied with whatever comes his way, whether it is fat or lean, whether little or much — such is the way of Torah, etc., and it is acquired through minimal pleasure. Then he shall delight in the Lord, and then “our mouths shall be filled with laughter” and the delight of our table shall be full of abundance, at the time when they shall say among the nations, “The Lord has done great things for these” (Psalms 126:2) — so may it be [His] will, speedily in our days, Amen.
Pele Yoetz 283:1: Onesh (Punishment) — The saying of Scripture is known (Proverbs 17:26), “Also to punish the righteous is not good.” And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 149b) that whoever causes his fellow to be punished is not brought into the divisions of the Holy One, blessed be He. And one who punishes and kills through curses does much harm. One harm is that he could have brought forth from him worthy offspring (and who could do as Moses our teacher did when he killed the Egyptian, as it is written [Exodus 2:12], “And he turned this way and that,” and our sages, of blessed memory, said [Shemot Rabbah 1:29] that he looked to the end of all generations, whether worthy offspring would come forth from him? And likewise Elisha when he cursed the youths [II Kings 2:24]). And there is more to it: that during his lifetime the person he cursed might have increased commandments and good deeds and given delight to his Creator, and at a time when the wicked is in distress, the Divine Presence is distressed — what does the tongue say? “I am pained in my head, I am pained in my arm.” And Rabbi Chaim Yosef David Azulai already wrote in the addenda to Sefer Devash LePi that what is written (Shabbat 34a), “He set his eyes on him and made him a heap of bones,” means that they would intend that if the wicked man deserved death and it was God's desire, the intention would take effect, and if not, not — in the manner of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, who took counsel with the angels when he killed the Egyptian (Shemot Rabbah 1:29). Or alternatively, “he set his eyes” means that the wicked man certainly deserved death. And the Tosafot (Bava Batra 22a, s.v. “Ana”) wrote regarding the saying “I caused his punishment,” that they used to grieve over this, for they said (Shabbat 149b) that whoever causes his fellow to be punished, etc. — see there.
Pele Yoetz 283:2: Thus it is fitting for a person to forgive everyone and seek mercy that no one be punished because of him. And there is another reason to seek mercy on this: so that he himself be saved from sin, for it is very difficult to escape transgressing what Scripture said (Proverbs 24:17), “When your enemy falls, do not rejoice.” And it is written (ibid. 17:5), “He who rejoices at calamity will not go unpunished.” And if he himself is saved, it is possible that his fellow will not be saved from the sin of suspecting the innocent, suspecting him of rejoicing at his misfortune, in such a way that one who curses his fellow and seeks his harm causes harm to himself. And just as they said (Rosh Hashanah 16b) that one who informs against his fellow to authorities is punished first, so it is with this matter: one who seeks his fellow's punishment for having sinned against him — the accusers will say, “Master of the world, it was he who sinned against You, all the more so does he deserve punishment.” Against this, one who overlooks his own grievances, they overlook all his transgressions for him (Yoma 23a).
Pele Yoetz 283:3: But it is fitting for the heads of the people in every place to punish sinners with bans, excommunications, and beatings through gentiles, fines and public shaming according to the sin and the need of the hour, so that the wicked man forsake his way and all the people hear and fear, and so that it serve as an atonement. And let the one punished accept the punishment with a pleasant countenance, knowing with certainty that they are doing good for him, for they said (Tanchuma, Mishpatim 5) that when there is no judgment below, there is judgment above. And through the little that is done to him, they save him from a worse punishment and spare him the many pains destined for the wicked. And how good is his portion, since through him many turn from sin and the children of iniquity no longer continue to transgress as before, and it turns out that he brings merit to the many, and the merit of the many depends on him. Go and learn from Zelophechad the righteous, who committed a transgression for the sake of Heaven and desecrated Shabbat in order to be killed (Tosafot, Bava Batra 119b), so that all the people would hear and fear.
Pele Yoetz 283:4: And the wise man has his eyes in his head, and takes counsel within himself as to how it is fitting to discipline, and with what it is fitting to discipline, and whom it is fitting to discipline, so that he not go out to bad ways, and that no strife arise in the city, and that no mishap result — all according to the place and the time and according to what the person is, for a soft tongue breaks a bone (Proverbs 25:15). And let him inform the one being punished of his ways, that he is doing it for his benefit, to repair his soul and atone for him for having sinned against his soul, and let him precede with prayer before the Lord that He guide him with good counsel and that no mishap result from his hand; and thereby the Lord will grant favor and honor, and will not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.
Pele Yoetz 284:1: Etzah (Counsel) — One who listens to counsel is wise, and salvation lies in an abundance of counselors (Proverbs 11:14), and how good it is for a person to have a good friend who will inform him of his counsel; and let him not rely on his own understanding, for every man is a liar, and two are better than one (Ecclesiastes 4:9), and even the great should take counsel from the small, as we find with the Holy One, blessed be He, who said (Genesis 1:26), “Let us make man,” and took counsel with the ministering angels, to teach man knowledge that where there are no great and elderly people, he should take counsel from the young; but it must be a trustworthy friend of his, for if not, it is better not to take counsel from him, lest he give him bad advice, or lest he give him good advice in innocence and he suspect the innocent and abandon his counsel, or he follow his counsel and it turns out badly for him and he comes to suspect him. And there is no more trustworthy friend for a man than his wife; therefore they said (Bava Batra 59b), “Your wife is short, bend down and whisper to her.” But since the minds of women are light, it is better to go to a sage from whom one benefits counsel and wisdom, and take counsel from him, that he advise fitting counsel according to the Torah, and according to what is right with good understanding. And presumably any Torah scholar is trustworthy in spirit, concealing a matter, and gives good and fitting counsel, even if he had a stake in the matter, and certainly the rabbi, since he is not a merchant, has no stake in the matter.
Pele Yoetz 284:2: And it is fitting for a person to give good counsel with all his heart even to his enemy, as written in Sefer Chasidim (section 134), whether in order to fulfill his duty to Heaven, or because his fellow might suspect him and abandon his counsel and do the opposite, and thereby take revenge upon him. And even if benefit for his fellow results in harm to himself, he should not worry, for as a reward for this the Lord will repay him double good. And if he wishes to be concerned for himself, he should not, for this reason, give unfitting advice; rather, let him withhold himself from giving advice and say, “I have no counsel, go to another,” and let him listen to all the counsel and discuss the matter, and take counsel with his Maker and pray to Him that He guide him with good counsel from before Him, for the counsel of the Lord shall stand (Proverbs 19:21).
Pele Yoetz 285:1: Arev (Guarantor) — It is written (Proverbs 11:15), “He shall surely suffer harm who guarantees for a stranger.” And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Yevamot 109 approx.), “One evil after another shall come upon the guarantors of Zion, who act rashly [‘draw and thrust’]” — meaning that they demand payment from the guarantor first. And now, according to the custom of the world and the ordinance of the marketplace, all guaranteeing is nearly of this kind, for whoever takes a guarantor does not wish to go through legal proceedings with the borrower and seize his property, but rather, as soon as the borrower does not repay him, he immediately demands payment from the guarantor, since it was on his credit that he lent the money; and there are cases where they stipulate explicitly, “From whichever of the two I wish, I shall collect.” And it is true that this is a hard thing for a person, especially if he is in pressing circumstances himself and needs to spend his own money for others — his teeth will gnash and be consumed, and he will be astonished and regret a thousand times the good deed he did.
Pele Yoetz 285:2: And a person is found perplexed in this matter, for if two go together to another city for fairs, and one is asked whether he will act as guarantor for his fellow, if he says no, it cuts off his livelihood, since the lender will understand that he is not creditworthy for the loan; therefore he is compelled to enter into being a guarantor. But the straight path, one that is a glory to those who follow it, is not to enter into being a guarantor unless he first takes a pledge, or says to the lender, “Know that I do not act as guarantor even for the king, for this is what I have accepted upon myself because of swindlers,” and let him do so. And if his fellow comes to ask him to be his guarantor, if he has money, let him say to him, “Here it is for you” [i.e., lend it directly]; and if not, let him say to him words such as these, and publicize the matter so that all who see him recognize this about him and it does not seem harsh in their eyes. And it is not fitting for the lender to seek a guarantor from someone in the presence of the borrower, or to say to the borrower, “If you bring me so-and-so as guarantor, I will give it to you,” for thereby he forces his fellow to become a guarantor against his will, not for his own benefit, out of shame and honor and for the sake of peace — and this transgresses what the Torah said (Leviticus 19:18), “And you shall love your fellow as yourself” — “what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow” (Shabbat 31a). Rather, if he wishes, let him go without the borrower present and without his knowledge and ask him, “Are you willing to be a guarantor for so-and-so? For otherwise I do not wish to lend to him.” And if he says he does not wish to be a guarantor, then let him say to the one who wishes to borrow, “I will only give it on my own terms; at sea I am not willing to be [without security]” [a wordplay]. And if you have guaranteed for your fellow, hasten to pay him, for if you do not wish to pay, your fellow's anger will burn against you more than if you yourself owed him a debt of your own, for regarding your own debt he will say, “What can the child do, since he needed to borrow and has nothing to repay,” but regarding a guarantee he will say to you, “Why did you trouble me? What business did you have entering into this dispute to be a guarantor, since it was on your credit that I lent to him? It turns out that you wanted to benefit my friend and harm me — why would you do this? One life is not pushed aside for another; you should have taken a pledge from the start, and if you trusted him, what concern is that of mine? Were it not for you, I would not have trusted him and would not have lent to him at all.” Thus the right and good thing is that he not push the lender to go through legal proceedings with the borrower and seize his property, but rather pay him immediately and himself seek repayment from the borrower. And on the other hand, if he did not explicitly become a guarantor, but rather was a partner or they borrowed together on one document, and one of them paid his share and the other did not pay, it is not the way of the good and the paths of the righteous to demand the other under the law of guarantorship, for what did he do and what should he have done, and it suffices that he stand by his own share. This is a great principle for one who wishes to conduct business with integrity: that he not follow strict law but rather what is right, and thereby he will find favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man.
Pele Yoetz 286:1: Erech (Assessment/Value) — Behold, all matters of serving the blessed Name require assessment: which is the straight path so that his reward not come out as his loss. For example, those who stand in the house of the Lord at night should see whether they can stand without sleep overtaking them during the Shema and prayer; and if he does not sleep during the day, he will come to sleep during the evening prayer and Grace after Meals, in which case the loss far outweighs the gain. Likewise, if one studies while dozing, half asleep and half awake, this is toil for nothing, and absence is better than a bad presence, and a little with intention is better (Tur and Shulchan Aruch, sec. 7, para. 14 approx.), and this is comparable to what people say, that the miser thinks to gain one and spends four — so this one thinks to gain one commandment and loses several times over. One must always see that the addition increases the essential thing rather than causing its loss, and that he not lose the coin for the sake of the small change. Likewise one must assess and distinguish between good and better — for example, regarding study, let him choose according to his understanding and according to his available free time which study is more important to study, such as the necessary laws, a word fitly spoken, or the laws of the sacrificial order, which is very important before the Omnipresent, or ethical books and the fear of the Lord; and if his free time allows, let him hold to this and also to that, and let his hand be in everything.
Pele Yoetz 286:2: Likewise, when he spends his money on a matter of a commandment, let him assess which commandment is more important before the Omnipresent. And the saying of the Yerushalmi is known (Shekalim, end of ch. 5) regarding those synagogues, where he said, “How many souls did your ancestors sink here — were there not people who could have occupied themselves with Torah?” And especially one whose means do not allow for great generosity should see on what he spends his money, that it be for the most important commandment, like a good merchant who seeks to invest his money in merchandise that yields the greatest profit. Only if the Lord has widened his boundary, let his hand be in everything, and let him open his hand wide to give to all the community funds and consecrated causes, and to be a groomsman and sandak and the like — whatever is in his power to do, let him do, and it is good for a man to manage his affairs with judgment.
Pele Yoetz 287:1: Aniyut (Poverty) — Poverty is a great trial for a person, for the evil of the poor man is great, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Ecclesiastes Rabbah, end of ch. 7), “Lack of money is harder than all of them,” for he wanders asking, “Where is bread?” The world has grown dark for him, and “the children beg for bread; no one breaks it for them” (Lamentations 4:4); and in his house there is no bread, no garment, and no penny in his pocket, empty upon empty, as the equal measure would have it, and creditors press him and the landlord presses him for the rent — woe from within, woe from without, one evil after another, trouble upon trouble, and many quarrels come upon him, and he is among the insulted, despised and ceasing to be a man, and the wisdom of the poor man is despised and his words are not heeded, and he is needy and desirous of everything, and his soul is dry, lacking everything, and many other such evils and troubles pass over the soul of the poor man that several exiles could not contain. In sum, all the days of the poor are evil, and bitter as wormwood and gall. This is his comfort in his poverty: knowing that through his poverty he escapes the province of Gehinnom, and better is one hour of tranquility of spirit in the World to Come than all the life of this world (Avot 4:17). And let him take to heart: is it conceivable that the Judge of all the earth would not do righteous judgment, God forbid, and show favoritism among children, giving one to eat to satisfaction and to cover himself abundantly and delight in abundance, while leaving another in hunger and thirst, naked and lacking everything? Heaven forbid that God be wicked or the Almighty do injustice; rather certainly the Rock, His work is perfect, for all His ways are justice, and His dealings are measured with purpose, and without any doubt it is done for his own good, and the reward is according to the pain, forever, his understanding being good, and happy is he if he withstands the trial and does not complain against His ways, blessed be He, but accepts everything with joy and gladness of heart, and over every trouble that comes he shakes his head and says, “This too is for the good.” And let him say, “If this is fitting before God, blessed be He, how much more so before me,” and let him consider that the flame has fallen even on cedars — upon the holy ones who are in the land, the geniuses of the world passed through days of poverty, pressure and pain, as explained in the Talmud and Midrashim, such as Hillel (Yoma 35b) and Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat (Megillah 28a; Bava Batra 10a), and complete men, and likewise many others who had many more evils and troubles pass over their heads than he has, and he is no better than they. Let him walk in his integrity as a righteous man, and let his poverty not cause him to transgress his Maker's will — let him not steal, deny, commit injustice, or speak falsely, for it is better for a person to die of hunger than to be wicked before the Omnipresent for even one hour. And the Lord will not withhold good from those who walk in innocence, for He feeds and sustains from the horns of wild oxen to the eggs of lice, and gives bread to all flesh, for His kindness endures forever (Psalms 136:25). And when he sits idle, let him not be among those who sit at street corners and engage in gambling, nor among the wine-guzzlers and strong-drink drinkers, in the manner of many ignorant poor people who waste their days in vain and their years in confusion, wandering here and there in the marketplaces and streets and idle gatherings for lack of anything, and in order to relieve their distress they increase drinking and waste money they do not have and come to disgrace, closing the gates of mercy before themselves, for the rich man will say, “Why should I give charity to this drunkard?” and they do not wish to know that he does it to relieve his distress, and that this alone is his clothing, it is his garment for his skin, this is the delicacy and delight of his soul. Be that as it may, not every person judges every person favorably, and man becomes a fleeting spirit, and who can restrain his words? And in truth, drinking is a chronic evil, destroying both soul and body, evil for Heaven and evil for humanity, evil for this world and evil for the World to Come, as written in its place, and thus the poor man inherits a double Gehinnom, Heaven have mercy.
Pele Yoetz 287:2: But let the poor man boast in this: that if he can earn, by the sweat of his brow he shall eat bread and not be dry [dependent] nor ashamed to do menial work, as Rav said to Rav Kahana, “Skin a carcass in the marketplace and take your wage, and do not say, ‘I am a kohen, I am a great man’” (Pesachim 113a). And great is one who benefits from his own labor, of whom it is said (Psalms 128:2), “When you eat the labor of your hands, happy are you and it is well with you” (Berachot, beginning of ch. 8). And let him not cast himself upon the community to be easily supported by charity; rather let him press himself and be troubled and it will be well for him, for they said (Shabbat 118a), “Make your Shabbat like a weekday rather than become dependent on people.” And they said (Pe'ah, end of ch. 8), “Whoever needs to take [charity] and does not take it will not die of old age until he supports others.” And let him not complain against the wealthy or bring a case of judgment against them, but rather seek from the One to whom wealth and possessions belong, and believe with complete faith that the key of livelihood is in the hand of the Creator, blessed be His Name, and He gives strength to do valiantly, and He places it in the wealthy man's heart and prepares for the poor man his livelihood through him, and the Omnipresent has many agents.
Pele Yoetz 287:3: Therefore let it not be heavy upon him to make his request of the wealthy man, and let it not seem harsh in his eyes if he sends him away empty-handed; rather let him picture himself as one who goes to the king's treasurer and asks him whether the king has sent through him his own portion and provision, and if he tells him no, let him not blame the treasurer, for he will say, “What is it to me? He was not privileged that the king desired to make him his agent, an agent of a commandment, and behold, He shall send it through others, for is there any shortage in the king's house of many agents and many means?” So it is with this matter, for a person's sustenance is fixed for him from Rosh Hashanah (Beitzah 16a). And if he needs to depend on others, let him not increase expenditures on pleasures and fine clothing, for people will speak wrongly of him and say, “See a man who does not need to take, yet takes,” and “why should we give charity to such a man, who is like one casting water into the sea?” And all the more so if he has creditors, he must be careful and guard against making expenditures and appearing to be wealthy, for people will speak wrongly of him and gnash their teeth. Therefore, if it happens to him that he finds an opportunity to buy cheaply something worth a hundred for one, let him not desire it and not buy it; and if he does buy it, let him turn around and sell it and profit, and let him not dress or clothe himself beyond what he has, and let him not display himself, for not everyone knows how it came to his hand, and he transgresses “you shall not place a stumbling block before the blind” (Leviticus 19:14).
Pele Yoetz 287:4: And when he cannot find a way to earn and profit, let him engage in Torah, for its merchandise is better than the merchandise of silver. In any case, even if the rope of poverty pursues him, dragging its children along, and he is in very pressing circumstances and has much business to attend to, nevertheless he should not fail to pray with the congregation morning, afternoon, and evening, and day by day and night by night fix times for Torah, whether little or much as he can, for every person is obligated only according to his own measure, and both the one who does much and the one who does little [are equal], etc. Woe, let him seek the honor of his house and the peace of his house, and since there is no penny in his pocket, let there be sweetness in his mouth and a sweet palate, and let him appease [his wife] with a gentle tongue through words, and tell her his trouble and pour out his soul, and say to her, “If I had it, I would make you a city of gold,” and better a dry morsel with quiet than [a house full of feasting with strife].
Pele Yoetz 287:5: And if it seems to him that in another city he could find a livelihood, let him not acquire a master for himself, for our sages, of blessed memory, said (Bava Metzia 75b) that whoever acquires a master for himself cries out and is not answered. And they explained this to mean one who is ashamed [to leave] in this city and does not go to another city; therefore let him wear down his feet and go from his land to wherever he can find rest that will be good for him for the service of the blessed Name. But let him not go out alone to wander about cities and leave his household behind, for as our own eyes see, this involves much trouble and little accomplishment, and in the end it does not succeed; rather this is the straight path, that he seek a place to settle with his household where he can find a way to earn and profit, whether through a craft or through trade, or by serving an individual or the public and the like, and let him not worry about being separated from his land and his birthplace — all this is vanity compared to the benefit of not wandering for bread, and of being settled to serve his Creator. And let him pour out his soul before the Lord, that He help him withstand his trial and provide his livelihood for him. These are some points of the straight path for the poor man in his poverty, and thereby he shall merit abundant good in a world where his understanding is good, and find means of his own redemption.
